edges.description: Loss of the cone CNG channel eliminates cone light responses.
Loss of cone transducin signaling prevents cone light responses.
Loss of PDE6C-mediated cGMP hydrolysis prevents the normal cone light response.
Loss of inhibitory PDE6H regulation disrupts the cone PDE6 response and cone phototransduction.
Cone dysfunction is associated with variable age-related structural change, but the responsible intermediates and individual trajectory are not fully resolved.
Loss of cone-mediated color discrimination causes the characteristic pan-axis color vision defect.
Loss of cone-rich foveal function reduces central visual acuity, with severity depending on residual cone function.
Loss of cone-mediated photopic adaptation produces marked light intolerance.
Poor foveal cone function prevents stable fixation during infancy.
Loss of cone phototransduction abolishes or markedly reduces photopic ERG responses.
Loss of central cone-mediated sensitivity produces a small central visual-field defect in some individuals.
Foveal cone loss and outer retinal disruption are observed as abnormal foveal morphology on OCT.
Dysregulated ATF6 signaling disrupts cone development, producing near-absent cone structure, foveal hypoplasia, and cone dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: The disease is caused by mutations in genes encoding crucial components of the cone phototransduction cascade (CNGA3, CNGB3, GNAT2, PDE6C, and PDE6H) or in ATF6, involved in the unfolded protein response.

nodes.description: ATF6 is a key ER stress sensor and transcription factor in the unfolded protein response (UPR). Biallelic ATF6 mutations cause achromatopsia through a mechanism distinct from phototransduction cascade defects. Pathogenic variants dysregulate the ATF6 arm of the UPR rather than abolishing the whole response. Human data establish an essential role in cone development, with near-absent cone structure, foveal hypoplasia, and cone dysfunction.

nodes.description: The cone cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channel is a heterotetrameric complex composed of three CNGA3 alpha subunits and one CNGB3 beta subunit. In darkness, high cGMP levels keep CNG channels open, maintaining a depolarizing dark current. Light-driven phototransduction reduces cGMP, closing channels and hyperpolarizing the cone. Biallelic pathogenic variants in CNGA3 or CNGB3 severely impair or abolish channel function and cone light responses. This is the most common mechanism, with up to 90% of patients carrying variants in CNGA3 or CNGB3.

nodes.description: PDE6C encodes the catalytic alpha prime subunit of cone cGMP phosphodiesterase. Activated cone transducin normally stimulates PDE6 to convert cGMP to 5-prime-GMP, lowering cGMP and closing CNG channels during the light response. Loss of PDE6C catalytic function impairs cGMP hydrolysis, favoring persistently elevated cGMP and open CNG channels and preventing a normal cone light response.

evidence.reference_title: Homozygosity mapping reveals PDE6C mutations in patients with early-onset cone photoreceptor disorders.
evidence.snippet: The PDE6C gene encodes the cone alpha subunit of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) phosphodiesterase, which converts cGMP to 5'-GMP, and thereby plays an essential role in cone phototransduction.

nodes.description: PDE6H encodes the inhibitory gamma subunit that restrains cone PDE6 catalytic activity until light-activated transducin relieves that inhibition. PDE6H loss therefore has the opposite predicted biochemical direction from PDE6C catalytic loss: reduced inhibition can favor excessive basal PDE6 activity, lower cGMP, and CNG-channel closure. That biochemical direction has not been directly established in affected humans; altered PDE6-complex stability or compensatory inhibition could modify it.

evidence.snippet: encoding the inhibitory γ subunit of the cone photoreceptor cyclic guanosine monophosphate phosphodiesterase.

nodes.description: Loss of cone phototransduction, or ATF6-dependent cone development, reduces or abolishes cone-mediated color and high-acuity photopic vision from infancy. This functional cone failure explains achromatopsia, reduced acuity, photophobia, and impaired fixation. Some cohorts also show variable age-associated structural abnormalities, although visual acuity is usually stable over time.

evidence.reference_title: Achromatopsia: Genetics and Gene Therapy.
evidence.snippet: The loss of cone photoreceptor function manifests at birth or early in childhood and results in decreased visual acuity, lack of color discrimination, abnormal intolerance to light (photophobia), and rapid involuntary eye movement (nystagmus).

nodes.description: GNAT2 encodes the alpha subunit of cone transducin, a heterotrimeric G protein that couples activated cone opsin to phosphodiesterase activation. Loss of GNAT2 function prevents signal transduction from photoactivated cone opsin to PDE6C, blocking the phototransduction cascade at the G-protein coupling step. cGMP levels remain constitutively high, but without transducin signaling the cone cannot generate a light response.

nodes.description: Subretinal delivery of AAV8 vectors carrying wild-type CNGA3 cDNA under a cone-specific promoter (human cone arrestin ARR3 promoter). Published phase I data show modest within-eye outcome signals, but the small, nonrandomized study cannot establish a causal efficacy effect. Active and completed phase 1/2 programs support continued clinical study, but CNGA3 gene augmentation remains investigational rather than approved therapy.

nodes.description: Subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of CNGB3 aims to restore cone CNG channel function. Preclinical studies in CNGB3-mutant dogs demonstrated stable restoration of cone function for at least 33 months. In the first-in-human NCT03001310 report, inflammation occurred in nine of 23 participants. It was mainly mild or moderate, but severe cases occurred primarily at the highest dose and two events were serious and dose limiting. No consistent group-level efficacy pattern was observed at 24 weeks. Human phase 1/2 programs remain investigational.

nodes.description: Visual acuity is often 20/200 or worse in complete achromatopsia, as central vision depends primarily on cone-rich foveal photoreceptors. Incomplete achromatopsia can be milder, with residual cone function and acuity as good as 20/80 in some individuals. Rod-mediated vision provides only peripheral and low-resolution input.

nodes.description: Achromatopsia is predominantly stationary with respect to best-corrected visual acuity, but some cross-sectional OCT cohorts show age-associated foveal hyporeflective zones and outer nuclear layer thinning. These findings support variable structural change without proving increased cell death or implying clinically progressive disease in every individual.
